title: "The Case for Operando Techniques"
author: "Your Name"
date: "2026-11-21"
categories: [hydrogen, electrolysis, AEMWE, research]
bibliography: references.bib
description: "Why single cell testing of anion exchange membrane water electrolysers needs to be enhanced with reference electrodes and operando X-ray imaging."
---

Alkaline water electrolysis using an anion exchange membrane (AEM) has been the focus of a great deal of research in recent years, because of the need to reduce the cost of electrolytic hydrogen [@Du2022Anion-ExchangeElectrolyzers; @Miller2020; @Vincent2018; @Lopez-Fernandez2021; @Santoro2022WhatFuture]. AEM water electrolysis (AEMWE) has distinct advantages over the more established alkaline water electrolysis (AWE) and proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE) technologies. If realised, AEMWE would have the low capital cost advantage of AWE, by leveraging inexpensive iron and nickel cell components, while having the flexibility, high current density and high pressure capabilities of PEMWE thanks to a polymer membrane electrolyte. Thus, solving the challenge of durability that AEMWE currently faces is of great interest and importance.

Making AEMWE technology a commercial reality requires the development of electrocatalysts, membranes and porous transport layers, among other cell components. Much of the recent AEMWE literature has focused on new materials like catalysts and membranes. These materials are often characterised ex situ and tested in traditional wet cells, using a rotating ring disc electrode setup for example. While these tests are important for a basic understanding of novel materials, testing with a single cell with a full membrane electrode assembly (MEA) is needed to truly understand how materials will perform under realistic electrolyser conditions.

There are, however, many issues with current single cell testing methods. Certainly, a lack of standardised and reproducible testing is a big challenge acknowledged by the community, and it prevents results reported from different laboratories from being reliably compared [@Du2022Anion-ExchangeElectrolyzers; @Miller2020; @Xu2022AnionEvaluation; @Lee2022AnionProduction; @Henkensmeier2021; @Titheridge2024TheElectrolyzers]. Progress has been made, with the European Union Joint Research Centre publishing harmonised protocols for testing low temperature water electrolysers in 2021 [@Tsotridis2021EUElectrolysers], but uptake of these guidelines has been slow and most laboratories still report their own test protocols. The JRC has since proposed harmonised accelerated stress testing protocols for low temperature water electrolysers [@Malkow2024EUElectrolyser], and inter-laboratory round-robin studies, in which several laboratories test identical materials and hardware using the same protocol, have begun to quantify the scale of the problem. Within Task 30 Electrolysis of the International Energy Agency's Advanced Fuel Cells Technology Collaboration Programme, round robins have established reference hardware and protocols for PEMWE [@Bender2019InitialElectrolyzers; @Lickert2023AdvancesHardware] and liquid alkaline electrolysis [@Appelhaus2024BenchmarkingElectrolysis]. AEMWE has lagged behind, and the first multi-laboratory single cell AEMWE round robin found that both in-house and cross-lab variation were even greater than for PEMWE, with cross-lab differences of up to 476 mV at 1 A cm^-2^ in pure water, compared with a maximum of 27 mV in the first PEMWE round robin [@Kreider2026Anion-exchangeTesting; @Bender2019InitialElectrolyzers]. Many studies that investigate new catalysts and membranes do publish MEA testing procedures and data, but the complexity of single cell electrolyser tests means experimental design varies significantly between research groups. Aside from the obvious differences of catalyst, ionomer and membrane, different porous transport layers, feed solutions and MEA fabrication techniques may be used, along with a multitude of other variables. Furthermore, many papers neglect to publish the full detail of their testing, making their work challenging to reproduce [@Smith2022ErrorTechnologies]. As a result, comparing the performance of novel catalysts and membranes from different studies is challenging.

If the benefit of single cell testing is the ability to see how new materials and components will perform and degrade in a real electrolyser, the drawback is the limited information that can be acquired during the test. Most single cell tests are limited to two-electrode electrochemical characterisation, including polarisation curves, impedance spectroscopy and cyclic voltammetry. These techniques are powerful, but they probe the cell as a whole, so distinguishing between processes related to each cell component can be challenging. This means that extensive testing of different MEAs is required, changing only one variable at a time, to narrow down the exact cause of performance differences. Post-mortem analyses of the cell components, like electron microscopy and X-ray spectroscopic techniques, help reveal the physical and chemical changes to the cell but necessitate its disassembly, which means the information obtained is less relevant to the materials within a real operating electrolyser.

Single cell testing can, however, be enhanced by additional electrochemical measurement devices such as reference electrodes, as well as by complementary in situ and operando imaging and spectroscopic techniques in specially designed test fixtures. By correlating different complementary measurements made during each electrolyser test, it is possible to achieve a richer and more detailed understanding of the processes occurring during electrolyser operation. Such an understanding is necessary for the advancement of electrolyser technology.

In my PhD, I used two different techniques to enhance single cell measurements: in situ reference electrodes and operando X-ray microtomography. By using an in situ reference electrode, the anode and cathode of the same MEA could be studied simultaneously in a three-electrode measurement that deconvolutes the half-cell potentials from the overall cell potential [@Malone2026EvaluatingElectrolysers]. Operando X-ray microtomography, meanwhile, enabled the physical changes to the internal structure of the electrolyser cell to be observed and correlated with changes in electrochemical performance [@Malone2025DeconvolutingMicrotomography].
